item.title: Dozens of Unexplained Drones Have Buzzed America's Nuclear Plants Since 2024
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Slashdot reader ElectricVs shares this report from American Buildout, a new site covering "the intersection of data centers, energy and power, finance, and Main Street."
Dozens of unexplained drones flew over and near U.S. nuclear facilities between February 2024 and March 2026, according to records the Nuclear Regulatory Commission made public this week. In all, facility operators filed 67 reports of drones over or near 28 sites in 17 states. They include the Three Mile Island site near Middletown, Pennsylvania., where Constellation Energy plans to restart Unit 1 as the Crane Clean Energy Center. In one incident, about five drones flew roughly 100 feet above the [970-megawatt] reactor building at River Bend Station in Louisiana.
The story was first reported by the publication The Liberation Times. The NRC published the documents on its website in response to the publication's freedom of information request... Every entry carries the status "Closed Unresolved." "Most of the incidents happened after dark," the article points out, "and none of the records identifies a drone operator. About half of the incidents, 33 of 67, occurred in an eight-week window between Dec. 3, 2024, and Jan. 24, 2025." (Virginia's Surry Power Station experienced five different incidents in December of 2024, including one involving "at least eight drones in two waves.") 100 miles west of Chicago, "drone activity" continued for more than two hours at the Byron Nuclear Station, where two separate drones were reported. In Waterford, Connecticut, "security observed four drones flying back and forth..."
The article notes a 2024 paper from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission citing a 2019 analysis that "concluded U.S. plants had no risk-significant vulnerabilities that adversaries could exploit with commercially available drones to cause radiological sabotage, or theft or diversion of special nuclear material."

item.title: Flock Reinstalled Its Cameras After Another City Canceled Its Contract
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Earlier The Drive reported a police chief "had to direct his staff to disconnect the power cords from Flock cameras in Plymouth, Minnesota after Flock Safety ignored and failed to respond to the department's notice the city was canceling its service. "But in other instances Flock's gone and reinstalled cameras without permission," The Drive reported this week:
On September 29th the city of Dayton, Minnesota posted a community update on its Facebook page alerting residents that Flock had installed and put into service two cameras against the City's direction without authorization... "The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City's direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization." The statement continued and noted, "Following the report, City staff reviewed locations throughout the community to determine whether any additional cameras had been reinstalled, and one additional location was identified. The Police Department has been notified, and both cameras will be removed promptly...."
The Minnesota cities of both St. Paul and Crystal told Kare 11 that they removed the Flock cameras themselves following their respective city council votes in August and September respectively. The cameras are stored and are still waiting to be picked up by Flock. Crystal Chief of Police Pete Underthun told Kare 11, "Once we made this decision, I personally went to the locations and removed the cameras and poles myself." Chief Underthun noted, "We are still working with the company to close out our contract and for them to pick the cameras up from our garage."

item.title: The AI-Bubble Scorecard
item.author: TheLLMSeeker
item.content:encoded: "AI bubble" had one of its loudest weeks of the year. CoreWeave slid to a new 52-week low on financing worries, Nvidia fell 4.4% on October 22, and Ken Griffin told a Citadel conference investors are "almost certainly" in a bubble, which promptly drew pushback from Deutsche Bank's Christian Sewing and BlackRock's Larry Fink. Jensen Huang, meanwhile, said neocloud demand is off the charts, but capital for them is scarce.I kept a score of all the pieces I saw this week, so 21 articles, reports, and columns from October 16 to 23 that came up in my searches with enough text to judge. Each piece is scored on its overall verdict: if it says AI is a bubble and/or about to pop; if it rejects the label or says burst fears are premature; if it presents both sides or says a bubble exists but isn't about to burst.Result: 8 bubble · 4 not a bubble · 9 mixed (21 pieces)Oct 16, Open Markets Institute: report on circular financing says the AI bubble is "primed to pop." Oct 16, IoT Analytics: analysis concluding there's no widespread AI bubble. Oct 17, Fortune: Wall Street debates whether the warnings are a head fake. Oct 17, The American Bazaar: the bubble "isn't bursting, it's being audited." Oct 18, Bloomberg: billionaires warn of a bubble, Howard Marks unconvinced. Oct 19, CEPR (Dean Baker): AI Bubble Monitor #19 Oct 20, NPR / WBUR: Is the AI boom a bubble waiting to burst? Oct 20, Bloomberg: Griffin says AI is "almost certainly" a bubble. Oct 21, 24/7 Wall St. (via Yahoo Finance): Griffin's bubble remarks. Oct 21, Bloomberg: Federated Hermes CIO says the boom has years to run. Oct 21, Bloomberg: Sewing and Fink push back on Griffin. Oct 21, Axios: The AI trade gets a reappraisal. Oct 21, Common Dreams: report warns the bubble is "primed to pop." Oct 21, The Blaze: Ed Zitron says the bubble is about to pop. Oct 21, Investing.com: Yardeni says a bubble exists but isn't about to burst. Oct 21, Investing.com: "AI bubble or not," manage the risk. Oct 21, Around Prague: a 16% weekly drop is a correction, not a collapse. Oct 22, CounterPunch: is CoreWeave's bad week the beginning of the end? Oct 22, Luminix: the evidence for and against. Oct 23, Asia Times: report says the bubble is "primed to pop." Oct 23, Tech Diplomacy (Substack): boom-or-bubble roundup. The bubble narratives are more concentrated than it looks. Three of the eight entries cover the same Open Markets/Americans for Financial Reform report, and two cover the same Griffin remarks, so by distinct underlying argument it's closer to The bigger tell is the mixed column: the most common position this week was some version of Yardeni's line, that the conditions for a bubble are there (its new meter reads 83 out of 100) but the triggers that ended past booms are only partly present (34 out of 100). Almost nobody in the sample argued AI itself is overhyped as a technology; the fight is about debt, financing, and whether the spending pays back in time.Bloomberg (Oct 18, 20, 21), Fortune (Oct 17), Axios (Oct 21), NPR/WBUR (Oct 20), CEPR AI Bubble Monitor (Oct 19), Common Dreams (Oct 21), Asia Times (Oct 23), CounterPunch (Oct 22), The Blaze (Oct 21), 24/7 Wall St. (Oct 21), Investing.com (Yardeni; "AI Bubble or Not"), Around Prague, IoT Analytics, The American Bazaar (Oct 17), Luminix, Tech Diplomacy Substack (Oct 23), CNBC (Oct 22, Huang), The Motley Fool (Oct 22, CoreWeave/Nvidia closes)

item.title: Google's AI Overviews Lowered Reddit's Traffic. Its Stock Dropped 29%
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Reddit's stock plunged 29.22% on Friday, reports CNBC, its worst drop since becoming a public company in 2024.
Thursday Reddit reported a sales growth that was weaker than previous quarters, and also forecast weak sales for the quarter to come (below analysts expectations):
The report comes as the company has seen a shift in its search referral traffic with the rise of Google's AI Overview. In an interview with CNBC, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said search-referral traffic from Google went "down meaningfully in this quarter" due to AI... Multiple analysts downgraded the stock following Reddit's disappointing results, with Citizens noting that "search changes highlight the problem with selling content to Google" and that as referral problems worsen, uncertainty around user growth amid the login requirement switch "puts more pressure on user monetization."
Reddit's CEO also said that forcing users to login will help the company's advertising business. "Reddit is the last platform to provide basically unfettered logged-out access, and that's largely because of me. I've been holding that line."
"I think users will probably go through the same understanding that I have, which is that it's a sign of the times. It's an evolution of how these platforms work."

item.title: I Gave My App Away for Free — And It Almost Killed It
item.author: Epic Devs
item.content:encoded: Generosity is a marketing strategy. Unit economics is a survival strategy. Here is how my "Founder's Launch Program" saved my indie app.The best week of my indie life.It started with a stranger on Reddit.He'd tried my native notes app, , on his Xiaomi phone and left a comment: "Feels fast and nice. But there's some minor visual weirdness on my phone." I replied offering him a free 3-month Pro code as a thank-you for the feedback. He said yes. I generated the code in the Play Console, felt like a real company handing out a real perk, and went to sleep happy.Then came more. A fellow tester who cancelled his subscription on principle but still sent me bug reports with screenshots. A student from India who emailed: "I'm a student, so I can't afford it. If you could make a lifetime promo code available for me, I would be able to fully use it and provide suggestions and bug reports. Please 🙏"I granted him lifetime Pro in about two minutes. It felt amazing. People were using my app. People were to me. After six months of building native Kotlin Multiplatform code at night after my day job as a product manager, this was the part that finally felt real.I thought I was doing indie development right. I was doing indie development . Not mathematically.The math I refused to do.Here's the embarrassing part: I'm a product manager by day. I build business cases for a living. I would never ship a feature at work without a rough cost-benefit estimate.And yet at 1 a.m., I was handing out free Pro access to an app with AI features without ever opening a spreadsheet.So let me open it now, in public.What a free Pro user costs me:Every AI summary and smart web clip is a call to a third-party AI API. Pennies per call — but power users summarize a lot.Every synced note is compute, storage, and bandwidth on my cloud backend.Every 90-day code, and especially every grant, is a commitment to pay both of those bills for months or years.What a free Pro user pays me: $0.My actual revenue at the time: three paying subscribers. Single-digit monthly recurring revenue.The scary part wasn't that the number was big. It was that the number was — and big enough to bleed. A leak doesn't need to be a flood to sink a boat that isn't moving.Why free users felt like growth (and weren't).The indie playbook says: give things away early, collect feedback, build goodwill. And the playbook is right — partially.That Xiaomi tester? His free code paid for itself ten times over. He sent screenshots of two real bugs (a settings sheet clipped by system insets, a formatting popup buried under the soft keyboard), his exact device model, and unprompted pricing research: "I have a rule against using subscription-based services." That's the kind of intelligence money can't buy.But here's what nobody tells you: most free Pro users don't do that. They redeem the code, run a few AI summaries, and go quiet. No feedback. No review. No referral. Every summary they run is a cost with no return.The uncomfortable reframe I had to accept: a free user who costs you money every month is not an asset waiting to convert. It's a liability waiting for your motivation to run out.The Pivot: The Founder's Launch ProgramI realized I was trying to force a subscription model on a market that was screaming for a one-time purchase. Multiple users told me, in different words, the same thing: So instead of defending my subscription, I stopped fighting subscription fatigue and decided to price for it.I just launched the EpicNotes Founder's Launch Program. It is a one-time for the first 100 users.Here is why I structured it this way:It solves the subscription fatigue: Users pay once and own the Pro features (including the AI engine) forever. No monthly anxiety.It solves my unit economics: The upfront cash injection covers my API and server costs for the next year, giving me the runway to keep building without bleeding money every month.It builds a core community: The 100 "Founders" get direct access to me. Their feedback shapes the roadmap.If you are tired of bloated Electron wrappers and want a truly native, privacy-first notes app for Mac and Android, this is your chance to support an indie dev and lock in a lifetime license before the doors close. (Link to the Founder's Launch Program is in my bio/below).What I changed (the boring, unsexy fixes).1. I hard-paywalled the AI. The free tier now includes the full notes experience — writing, formatting, sync — but zero AI. AI is the only feature with a real marginal cost, so it's the only feature behind the paywall. A free user now costs me roughly the price of storage: pennies.2. I put my generosity on a budget. Twenty goodwill codes, total. They now go to people who give something back: detailed feedback, honest reviews, real reach. The tester who sends bug reports with screenshots? Instant yes. A drive-by "send code pls"? A polite no with a link to the free tier. I reached out to my core users and told them the truth: solo dev, real server costs, if this app helps you, here's how to keep it alive. Honesty converts better than guilt — and both convert better than silence.Generosity is a marketing strategy. Unit economics is a survival strategy. You need both — but in this order: survive first, then be generous .I'm still giving EpicNotes away to students, testers, and kind strangers on Reddit. I just open the spreadsheet before I open the billing dashboard now.If you want to try a native, local-first notes app without the subscription trap, grab a spot in the . Let's build the best productivity tool on the Mac and Android ecosystems together.Have you ever been burned by subscription fatigue? Tell me in the comments. And if you want to support an indie dev building native apps, check out EpicNotes below.https://epicapps.app/epicnotes

item.title: Two US Senators Raise Privacy Concerns About Meta's 'Pervert Glasses'
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Meta's smart glasses face new questions from two U.S. Senators, reports Gizmodo. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Sen. Edward Markey "are requesting that Meta provide more information before Thanksgiving on whether it conducted detailed human rights due diligence and safety testing on the product before releasing it," reports Gizmodo. The Senators also requested information from Meta about " how it evaluated the privacy risks posed by the glasses, and what kinds of safeguards are currently in place."
"Although Meta identified risks to bystander privacy and vulnerable populations before launching its glasses in 2021, it nevertheless launched a product tailor-made for invading the privacy of its users and bystanders," [the senators wrote in a letter Thursday...] The glasses have also been spotted on ICE agents during raids, and have raised potential surveillance concerns. The surveillance fears were even reportedly raised by the New York Police Department's counterterrorism unit in a memo issued earlier this year....
"Meta's own disclosures confirm that imagery processed through its glasses' visual AI features may be retained and used to train AI systems, including with the assistance of human reviewers," the senators' letter states, calling the practice an invasion of privacy. "Retaining that material for AI development, thereby extending the period during which it can be accessed, disclosed, or misused, exploits people's highly sensitive information for Meta's commercial benefit."

item.title: Supersonic Airliner In Doubt As Company Shifts to Powering AI Data Centers
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Boom Supersonic's plans to launch its Overture passenger jet by 2029 are facing growing doubts as the company pivots toward manufacturing natural gas turbines for AI data centers. Ars Technica reports: One of the company's first customers, United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, has expressed doubts about Boom's original plan to deliver the first Overture supersonic airliner in 2029. Kirby's latest frank assessment came during an interview with the Office Hours: Business Edition podcast that appeared on October 28, 2026. "'29 is their official timeline," Kirby told podcast host Monica Langley. "It's not going to happen in '29 -- it's going to take longer."
[...] Much of Boom's recent focus has been on developing natural gas turbines to power AI data centers as an additional revenue stream. On October 22, the company unveiled another factory in Centennial, Colorado, dedicated to producing a 42-megawatt natural gas turbine called Superpower for data centers. [...] Boom described its new Superpower factory as making turbine parts while still undergoing construction. It aims to deliver the first gas turbines to AI data center customers in mid-2027 while ramping up annual production to 25 turbines in 2028 and 50 turbines by 2029.
[...] Still, Boom has characterized the development of a gas turbine for data centers as being synergistic with its design of the Symphony engine for the Overture airliner. During the October announcement, it also described having completed a prototype turbine core, called Sprint Core, that is intended to eventually power both the Superpower gas turbine and Symphony engine for the airliner. That turbine core is set to undergo testing at the Colorado Air & Space Port, with Boom planning to fire the turbine for the first time before Thanksgiving. That would be a concrete development milestone, but the company still has much to do in proving it can get both its AI data center and supersonic airliner ventures off the ground.

item.title: What Is EIP-7702? Ethereum's Smart Account Feature Explained, and How to Stay Safe
item.author: MEXC Learn
item.content:encoded: On October 29, 2026, an Ethereum hot wallet belonging to Binance was emptied in a single transaction.The tool behind the drain was EIP-7702, a feature that went live on Ethereum in May 2025.As of October 30, 2026, no flaw in EIP-7702 itself has been reported.It did exactly what a valid signature told it to do, and that is the part worth understanding.● EIP-7702 lets a regular Ethereum wallet run smart contract code, and it went live on May 7, 2025.● A token approval covers one token for one app, while an EIP-7702 delegation hands a contract your whole account.● Every delegation needs the wallet’s own signature, so the Binance hack looks like a signing-side failure, not an Ethereum bug.● Exchange users should watch official notices, withdrawal status, proof of reserves and the post-mortem.● Self-custody users only face EIP-7702 risk if they signed a delegation, which Etherscan’s Delegated Address field shows.● A delegation can be reset to the zero address, but if you don’t remember signing it, treat the wallet as compromised.EIP-7702 is an Ethereum upgrade that lets a regular crypto wallet, known as an externally owned account or EOA, borrow smart contract code and behave like a smart account.It shipped with the Pectra upgrade, which went live on Ethereum mainnet on May 7, 2025.The official specification, EIP-7702: Set Code for EOAs, adds a new transaction type that carries signed “authorizations.”Each one names a contract and must be signed with the wallet’s own private key.It starts with a signature.You sign an authorization that names a contract, the chain it covers and your account’s nonce, which is simply a running count of your transactions.Any account can then submit that authorization to Ethereum, which is how a third party can pay the fee for you.Once it lands, the network writes a small pointer on your account, which the specification calls a delegation indicator.From then on, calls to your address run the code of the contract it points to, while your private key keeps full control of the account.To undo it, you sign a new authorization that points to the zero address, and the account goes back to being a plain wallet.How Does EIP-7702 Bring Account Abstraction to Wallets?Account abstraction is the push to make Ethereum wallets programmable instead of limited to one signature and one action at a time.EIP-7702 brings that idea to existing wallets, so nobody has to move funds to a new address.The specification names three uses:● several actions, such as approve and swap, in one all-or-nothing transaction● another account pays the network fee for you and can be repaid in a token other than ETH● a sub-key with narrow permissions, such as spending tokens but not ETHEach of these depends on the contract your wallet points to, which is why the next section matters.How Is an EIP-7702 Delegation Different From a Token Approval?A token approval lets one app move one token, usually up to a set amount.An EIP-7702 delegation hands the logic of your entire account to a contract, covering every asset inside it, until you reset it.That gap in scope is why a bad delegation does far more damage than a bad approval.Think of your wallet as a house.A token approval is like handing someone the key to one cabinet to take out one item.An EIP-7702 delegation is closer to hiring a house manager who runs every room.A good manager, like a reputable wallet app’s smart account contract, only follows your instructions.A malicious one can clear out the whole house in one trip.Your private key stays the master key, which also means anyone holding it can hire a new manager.What Happened in the Binance EIP-7702 Hack?On October 29, 2026, an attacker used signed EIP-7702 authorizations to point Binance’s Ethereum hot wallet at the attacker’s own contract.Minutes later, one transaction emptied it.Early on-chain estimates put losses across Binance’s wallets in the billions of dollars as of October 30, 2026.Public on-chain data shows four steps:● Around 20:20 UTC, a batch of authorizations signed with the wallet’s key landed on Ethereum.● The wallet’s nonce kept changing, so the batch reportedly covered many values, and the one that matched handed the wallet to the attacker’s contract.● About three minutes later, one call moved out ETH, stablecoins and dozens of other tokens.● Almost four hours later, the delegation was revoked.Step one is the key detail: a delegation needs the wallet’s own valid signature, so either the key itself leaked or a system that holds it signed when it should not have.Was It a Leaked Private Key or a Tricked Signing System?As of October 30, 2026, Binance had not published a root cause.Two explanations are on the table, pointing to very different weak spots.The first is a leaked private key, a familiar failure with a familiar fix: retire the key and lock down everyone who had access.The second is more unsettling.Many exchanges route hot wallet signing through automated services that check where funds are going and how much is moving.An EIP-7702 authorization is not a normal transfer.It is a short signed message naming a contract, with no recipient or amount for those rules to inspect.If a signing service approved one without decoding it, the exchange’s own security layer signed away control of the wallet.Early reports also described funds leaving on blockchains that have no EIP-7702 feature at all, which, if confirmed, would point to the signing side.Is My Money Still Safe on an Exchange After the Binance Hack?A hot wallet is only the slice of an exchange’s funds kept online for withdrawals.Whether customers are made whole depends on the exchange’s reserves and what it formally commits to, such as a protection fund, so trust official updates over social media posts.● Announcements on Binance’s own website and verified accounts● Deposit and withdrawal status for each network● An updated proof of reserves report● A post-mortem that names the root cause and the fixOn MEXC, users can confirm their own balance is included in the reserve data through a Merkle tree check.Should I Move My Crypto Off an Exchange After a Hack?A hack at one exchange does not automatically put your funds at risk, and moving them is a personal call.If you do move some, send a small test amount first and double-check the network and address before the full transfer.Does EIP-7702 Put My Own Wallet at Risk?Not unless you signed a delegation.Holding ETH in a self-custody wallet does not switch EIP-7702 on, and there is nothing to “upgrade.”Ethereum’s official site says anyone telling you to “upgrade” your ETH is trying to scam you.The real risk is phishing.A fake airdrop or website can ask you to sign an authorization that points your wallet at a malicious smart contract, disguised as a routine prompt.Etherscan’s guide to EIP-7702 smart accounts, published in June 2025, said over 97% of all delegations were linked to scams targeting vulnerable users.One more catch: an authorization signed with a chain ID of zero is valid on every EVM chain that supports EIP-7702, as the EIP-7702 guidelines on ethereum.org warn.How Do I Check and Revoke an EIP-7702 Delegation?Paste your address into Etherscan and find the Delegated Address field.“Null” means no delegation.If it shows a contract that isn’t your wallet app’s, reset it from inside the wallet.● A known wallet contract, such as MetaMask’s EIP-7702 Delegator, simply means you turned on that wallet’s smart account.● If you don’t recognize the contract, revoke it in your wallet app, which delegates to the zero address.● Repeat the check on other EVM chains where you use the same address.● If you don’t remember signing that delegation, assume your key or seed phraseis exposed and move everything to a new wallet.Revoking won’t rescue a wallet whose key has leaked, because whoever holds the key can sign a fresh delegation a minute later.Could an EIP-7702 Attack Happen Again?EIP-7702 is a finalized, live part of Ethereum, so the feature is not going away.The clearest fix sits with whoever controls signing: systems that decode every authorization and refuse any contract that isn’t pre-approved.The specification itself says there is no safe way to let apps request delegations freely.Is EIP-7702 a bug in Ethereum?No, it is an intended feature with Final status, and every delegation needs the wallet’s own signature.What is the difference between EIP-7702 and ERC-4337?Both move Ethereum toward account abstraction, but EIP-7702 upgrades an existing wallet while ERC-4337 relies on separate smart contract accounts.Which Ethereum upgrade added EIP-7702?EIP-7702 shipped in the Pectra upgrade, which activated on May 7, 2025.How do I revoke an EIP-7702 delegation?Sign a new delegation to the zero address from your wallet app, which resets the account to a plain wallet.Does an EIP-7702 delegation work on other chains?Only on the chain it names, unless it was signed with chain ID 0, which makes it valid on every EVM chain that supports it.Was EIP-7702 hacked in the Binance incident?As of October 30, 2026, no flaw in EIP-7702 had been reported, and the delegation carried the wallet’s own valid signature.Do I need to do anything with my ETH because of EIP-7702?No, your ETH needs no upgrade, and you only need to act if you find a delegation you don’t recognize.Is my money on Binance safe after the EIP-7702 hack?As of October 30, 2026, Binance had not published a root cause, so rely on its official announcements and proof of reserves rather than social media posts.The Bottom Line on EIP-7702EIP-7702 gives ordinary Ethereum wallets real smart account powers, and it also lets one signature hand over an entire account.The Binance hack showed that power at full scale, with no Ethereum bug reported as of October 30, 2026.Check your Delegated Address once, stay wary of any prompt to “upgrade,” and follow ETH on MEXC’s Ethereum price page.

item.title: France’s AI Strategy: Turning Models, Compute, and Public Investment Into National Capability
item.author: tt
item.content:encoded: France's potential role in AI rests on its ability to organise a chain of capabilities. Model developers can produce useful technologies, computing institutions can provide infrastructure, and public administrations can establish sustained demand. National capacity grows when these activities become connected through arrangements that work under practical constraints. The decisive question is whether French institutions can secure the resources they need, adapt them to their purposes and remain responsible for the resulting decisions.That question matters because the visible scale of an AI strategy can obscure its operational content. In February 2025, the Élysée reported €109 billion in announced investments associated with AI infrastructure and deployment projects. [1] This signalled commitments by investors. It was neither a measure of installed computing capacity nor a statement that the French state had already spent that amount. Assessing France requires following projects and access arrangements beyond the announcement.Models that users can adaptIn the Invention layer, an important distinction concerns what users can actually obtain and modify. Mistral's documentation lists Ministral 3 8B, released in December 2025, as generally available under Apache 2.0. [2] An available model with permissive licensing gives developers a different set of options from a service accessible only through a proprietary interface. It can support adaptation and deployment decisions closer to the institution using it.That possibility is not equivalent to a complete operating capability. An administration still needs suitable infrastructure, technical staff, evaluation procedures and authority to use the relevant data. A model that performs well on a general benchmark may require considerable work before it can support an administrative task reliably. The French opportunity is to develop those supporting capacities around models that institutions can understand, test and replace.Mistral's August 2026 announcement provides a useful illustration of access becoming more specific. The company said its regional endpoints were generally available, allowing customers to select inference in Europe or the United States. It also disclosed that limited, safeguarded transfers to subprocessors outside the selected region could occur. [3] This is evidence of a defined service offering, with stated limits. A European processing location alone cannot establish complete control over the surrounding technical and contractual relationships.Industrialisation requires infrastructure that can support demanding work at useful scale. Alice Recoque illustrates both the ambition and the institutional complexity. EuroHPC signed its procurement contract in November 2025. The planned system will be owned by EuroHPC and hosted in France, with GENCI managing the project and CEA operating the machine. The Jules Verne consortium includes the Netherlands and Greece, and computing resources are to be allocated jointly in proportion to investment. [4]France therefore occupies a significant organisational position without acquiring exclusive national disposal of the system. The planned architecture also combines European components with AMD processors and accelerators. [4] European coordination can enlarge access and influence while retaining external technological dependencies. The relevant policy issue is whether those dependencies remain manageable through procurement, support and continuity arrangements.Project timing is equally consequential. GENCI's current project page identifies the end of 2027 as the expected operational date. [5] This profile therefore treats Alice Recoque as contracted future capacity. It does not add its promised performance to a present French inventory. The distinction affects decisions by laboratories and public organisations that need resources before the new system becomes available.The state as an organised userOperationalisation becomes more tangible in Albert API. DINUM, France's interministerial digital directorate, operates this shared gateway to generative models. Its official description covers access to open-weight and proprietary models, alongside functions such as document classification, retrieval and optical character recognition. It identifies Albert API as an instance of the state-developed OpenGateLLM software. [6]A shared interface can help administrations avoid rebuilding the same connections and can make changing providers less disruptive. Its strategic value depends on the surrounding institutional arrangements: which data may be processed, who evaluates performance, how errors are corrected and who can suspend a failing service. DINUM's page states that an approved version for internal state data is still being finalised. [6] Claims about universal readiness for sensitive public workloads would therefore exceed the evidence.This is where governance connects Invention, Industrialisation and Operationalisation. The state can shape demand through procurement specifications and common infrastructure, while retaining responsibility for each public use. An architecture that permits model substitution, independent evaluation and continuity of service would make national capability less dependent on the fortunes of a single supplier. Achieving this requires administrative expertise as well as technical investment.Four developments would make France's trajectory easier to judge. First, documented acceptance and access milestones for Alice Recoque would establish when contracted infrastructure becomes usable. Second, reports on completed and energised facilities would distinguish delivered investment from announcements. Third, Albert API's authorisation status and service records would clarify which workloads it can responsibly support. Fourth, evaluations of public deployments would reveal whether AI improves accuracy, processing times or service quality at an acceptable cost.France could play a substantial European role by connecting model development, shared computing and public demand into dependable arrangements. The strongest evidence would be institutions that can continue to operate, evaluate and adapt their systems when suppliers, prices or political conditions change. That would demonstrate a capacity to mobilise AI for public purposes, extending the significance of the companies and infrastructure located within French territory.This is original country analysis applying the GOAI capability conversion framework. It is not a peer-reviewed country assessment or a scored ranking. Service characteristics reflect their providers' descriptions; expected dates remain forecasts.

Perfect memory, consistent values, and a thousand shared bodies are assumptions within that experiment, not measured capabilities of present-day AI systems.Suppose we have passed the crossing point in Chapter 4, and fidelity as described in Chapter 5 is high enough. item.title: Greece's AI Strategy: How DAEDALUS and PHAROS Could Shape Its Future
item.author: tt
item.content:encoded: DAEDALUS's inauguration in Lavrion on 19 October 2026 brings Greece's immediate AI policy question into sharper focus: how will institutions use the new computing base? EuroHPC and GRNET point to a delivered supercomputing installation, following earlier procurement and benchmark milestones. [1] This creates an opportunity for researchers, businesses and public organisations to attempt work that previously required different access arrangements. Its strategic significance will emerge through the projects that can use it reliably and the institutions able to retain the resulting expertise.The most plausible Greek role is selective. A country does not need to lead every part of the AI system to build useful capabilities. It does need to choose applications where computing resources, relevant data and responsible organisations can be brought together. For Greece, PHAROS identifies health, culture and language, and sustainability as priority domains. [2] These provide a focus for assessing outcomes rather than treating every new AI activity as evidence of national progress.Establishing what has been deliveredThe DAEDALUS timeline deserves precision. EuroHPC launched the tender in June 2024. EuroHPC announced the signed contract with Hewlett Packard Enterprise on 28 March 2025. In June 2026, the system appeared in the TOP500 ranking, while EuroHPC still described wider European availability as forthcoming. The October inauguration is a further milestone. [3–5, 1] These events establish different things: procurement, contractual commitment, benchmark performance and public inauguration should remain distinct in the record.At inauguration, EuroHPC reported sustained performance of 85.69 petaflops and peak performance of 115 petaflops. The system uses HPE infrastructure and more than 2,000 NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips. [1] Neither performance figure measures the quality of an AI model or the effectiveness of a public service. Benchmark capacity becomes useful to an organisation only when it has access, suitable software and people able to formulate and execute the work.Hosting, access and responsibilityDAEDALUS is operated by GRNET within an international arrangement. The procurement documentation states that access is jointly managed by EuroHPC and the DAEDALUS consortium in proportion to investment. The acquisition cost was €36 million, with 35% funded by EuroHPC and 65% through the EU-financed Greece 2.0 recovery plan; Cyprus, Montenegro and North Macedonia also participate in the consortium. [1, 4]This arrangement broadens the resources and relationships available to Greece. It also means that the machine's location does not give every Greek institution unrestricted or immediate access. Ministries, universities and firms need to understand the relevant allocation routes, eligibility conditions and support arrangements. A national strategy should therefore examine who can obtain useful computing time, how long applications take and whether users can continue their work after an initial project.External technological dependence also remains material. Hardware supplied by HPE and NVIDIA brings substantial capabilities, while tying parts of the system's operation and renewal to those suppliers. [1] The policy response should concern support continuity, staff competence and credible options for future workloads. Owning or hosting infrastructure cannot by itself remove dependence on the organisations that design and maintain essential components.PHAROS as the connection to useThe distinction between Invention, Industrialisation and Operationalisation helps locate the task. Invention includes the development of methods, models and specialised knowledge. Industrialisation supplies the infrastructure and repeatable technical processes needed to work at scale. Operationalisation concerns the sustained use of those capabilities in organisations. Governance connects the layers by determining access, data permissions, funding and accountability.PHAROS describes its purpose as connecting academia, industry and the public sector through computing infrastructure, services and expertise. [2] Its importance lies in that organisational connection. A research group may need help adapting software; a small firm may need technical guidance; a public agency may need a clear procedure for using data and evaluating results. These requirements differ, even when users share the same machine.For Greek-language applications, a plausible objective is better performance on particular public or professional tasks, supported by transparent evaluation. For environmental applications, it could be tools that improve a defined monitoring or planning process. In health, an initial priority could be carefully governed research workflows. These are proposed directions, not claims that PHAROS has already delivered those outcomes. Each requires an accountable institution and a plan for continuing the service after development funding ends.How to judge the next phaseFour indicators would make progress observable. First, published access and utilisation records should show which categories of users obtain computing time and whether access meets their needs. Second, completed projects should report task-specific results, including failures and costs. Third, repeated use by public bodies and firms should reveal whether initial demonstrations become sustained activity. Fourth, staff retention and maintained software should show whether technical knowledge remains available within the organisations using it.These indicators would also help direct resources. Heavy demand without sufficient support would suggest an implementation bottleneck. Available capacity with few viable projects would point towards weaknesses in project preparation, data access or institutional demand. The appropriate response would differ in each case. Aggregate computing performance cannot diagnose these problems.Greece can develop a meaningful role as a location for selected AI applications and regional collaboration if it converts the new infrastructure into dependable institutional capability. DAEDALUS provides a stronger starting point, and PHAROS offers a route for organising its use. The decisive evidence will be organisations that can solve relevant problems, maintain their systems and exercise responsibility for the consequences.This is original country analysis applying the GOAI capability conversion framework. It is not a peer-reviewed country assessment or a scored ranking. Future applications and project objectives remain distinct from delivered infrastructure.

item.title: Microduck, the Robot Pet That Imitates Life: Can We Really Grow Attached to a Machine?
item.author: Fabrizio Marozzo
item.content:encoded: Imagine a small robotic duck walking around your home, reacting to its surroundings, and even picking up small objects with its beak. When it simulates sadness, it lowers its head and makes soft, melancholic sounds. When it expresses happiness, it produces higher-pitched, lively sounds accompanied by body movements. Its name is .Standing just 25 centimeters tall and weighing less than 800 grams, it illustrates how advances in artificial intelligence and robotics are making increasingly sophisticated interactions between humans and machines possible.One of its most curious features is . Every Microduck has a unique sonic identity generated from its processor's serial number. As a result, no two units produce exactly the same sounds. It may seem like a minor detail, but it makes each robot recognizable, almost as if it had its own personality. Through different sounds and postures, Microduck can also simulate emotional states such as sadness and happiness.Of course, the robot does not actually experience these emotions: it reproduces their outward expressions. Yet, the effect can be surprisingly convincing to anyone watching. There is also another interesting aspect: . When two or more Microducks come together, they can interact and, when appropriately configured, even perform a kind of chorus. Their behavior resembles that of animals that live in groups and communicate with one another.But behind this playful appearance lies an enormous technological challenge. Microduck's software is , allowing developers to study how it works, modify it, and create new behaviors. Moreover, thanks to a and reinforcement learning, the robot can be trained in a virtual environment.There, it can experiment with thousands of movements, fall, correct its mistakes, and try again. Cloud computing makes it possible to run large numbers of experiments in parallel, something that would require considerable time, money, and resources in the physical world. Once learned, these behaviors can be transferred to the real robot, an approach commonly known as . This is how it can acquire unusual skills, such as learning to move on skates.Another major challenge is . Microduck is equipped with fifteen motors, sensors, and a compact computing system. A neural network helps control its movements, continuously adjusting its balance and position. All of this must run on a small battery, which provides limited autonomy. Nature has been dealing with similar challenges for millions of years: animals perceive their environment, react, and move using energy obtained from food.We tend to take these abilities for granted, yet reproducing them in machines remains extraordinarily difficult. Consider the complexity of developing increasingly autonomous robots capable of understanding instructions, reasoning about what to do, and translating decisions into precise physical movements. Combining artificial intelligence, perception, and physical action in small, affordable devices with limited energy consumption is one of the major technological challenges of the coming years.This brings us to an interesting question: why did Microduck's developers choose these particular characteristics? Its distinctive voice, simulated emotions, interactions with other robots, and amusing movements seem directly inspired by the animal world. The goal is probably not just to make the product appealing, but also to encourage an emotional connection with its users.A small robot like Microduck could anticipate a new generation of artificial pets, somewhere between intelligent toys and future household assistants.It could keep us company, entertain us, and learn new behaviors through our interactions. It would also offer several practical advantages: it does not make a mess, does not need to be taken outside, does not get sick, and never requires a visit to the veterinarian. If we leave home for a week, we can simply turn it off and find it exactly where we left it when we return.But a real pet is something profoundly different. A dog or a cat does not simply simulate emotions through a computer program. Animals are living beings, with instincts and biological needs, capable of experiencing pleasure, pain, and fear. They explore, seek companionship, and spontaneously react to what happens around them. They build relationships through experience, learning, and living together. The bond between humans and animals also develops through everyday care, shared habits, and trust built over time.Above all, having a pet means accepting responsibility. An animal can become sick, grow old, and suffer. It needs us even when we are tired, busy, or would rather be doing something else. A robot, on the other hand, may offer many of the enjoyable aspects of companionship without requiring the same sacrifices. And perhaps that is precisely one of the reasons why devices like Microduck could become successful.Yet there is a fundamental difference: simulating life is not the same as living it. An animal is not merely a collection of needs and responsibilities. It gives us affection, companionship, and moments of happiness. It gets to know us, recognizes our habits, and develops a relationship that changes over time.Caring for it, facing difficulties together, and even knowing that one day we will have to say goodbye are all part of that relationship. We cannot simply turn off an animal when it becomes inconvenient, because it is not an object at our disposal. It is a living being with whom we share part of our existence.But our relationship with an animal is only one part of its life. Every living organism belongs to a much larger cycle, in which different forms of life are interconnected and contribute to the balance of nature. Millions of years of evolution have shaped organisms capable of performing extraordinarily complex functions, often using surprisingly small amounts of energy and resources.A robot can imitate an animal's voice, movements, and even its emotional expressions, but it does not participate in this biological cycle as a living organism. However sophisticated it becomes, it remains a collection of circuits, motors, and silicon chips.Microduck is nevertheless an interesting technological achievement, showing how rapidly robotics is evolving, partly thanks to advances in artificial intelligence. I am convinced that similar devices will become successful and occupy an increasingly important place in our homes.Yet, I must admit that this prospect also raises some concerns, particularly about the relationships we may develop with them. Perhaps the most interesting question is not how closely robots will come to resemble animals, but how willing we will be to grow attached to something that appears alive without actually being alive.

item.title: Open-Sourcing All Day AI: The Playbook for a 12,000+ Attendee Conference
item.author: Brian Turcotte
item.content:encoded: All Day AI was a free, online, 16-hour marathon event with zero vendor pitches. We pulled it together in about two months, saw 12,313 participants and 140 speakers, and people stayed and watched for an average of more than 6 hours.An event of this scale doesn’t come together that fast without some serious sprinting, trial and error, and audible-calling. Plenty of people have asked how we did it, so this article open-sources the whole playbook: the goals, the team, the tools, the timeline, and the parts we’d change.We built All Day AI for people who were under pressure to put AI to work but struggling to find advice they could trust. The tools and recommendations were changing week to week, and a lot of the conversation still led back to something for sale. We wanted a place where practitioners could explain what they had actually shipped, what had failed, and what another team could reuse.That need shaped the format. Keeping the event free and online meant people could join from wherever they worked, without a ticket budget, a flight, or a travel approval. Banning vendor pitches kept the focus on useful lessons rather than a sales conversation. Across Build, Lead, Secure, and Ship, the goal was to give people clearer answers and peers they could keep learning with after the day ended.The first version of our website went up in August, and the event was slated to go live on October 22. That gave us roughly two months to hit our admittedly aggressive goals:What made those numbers hard was that we were starting from zero. There was no existing All Day AI community, no speakers signed up, no website, no event platform, and no social presence. Every registrant and every speaker had to come from something we built or someone we reached in those two months.If you’ve run an online event with multiple speakers, you know that even one track can be a logistical nightmare. We knew 120+ speakers across 4 tracks could get ugly, fast, so most of what follows is about how we kept it from getting ugly: a committed team, a few deliberate bets, and a lot of help from AI agents.The most important part of the ADAI stack was the people. The core organizing team had more than 20 people across event co-founders, moderators, hackathon judges, ushers, and marketers, and they worked quickly and unselfishly through the build-up and especially on the day of. The team brought experience from organizations including Anaconda, Matejczyk Group, Carnegie Mellon University’s Software Engineering Institute, Techstrong Group, ACI Worldwide, and Community Hackathons, produced by Crowdbyte Solutions.This was a community event, so all of it fell outside everyone’s day job. Nobody was paid to make All Day AI happen, and the fact that it happened anyway is a credit to how much the team believed in the project. They deserve not only credit but admiration.Before we picked a single tool, we made a few decisions about what kind of event this would be. Those decisions shaped everything else, and in hindsight they did more for our numbers than any piece of software. Most conferences exist with at least a subtle motivation of money changing hands. People can sense that, and when they just want to learn, it’s a turnoff. So we banned pitches from the jump. That gave us a simple promise to make to attendees and speakers alike: you’re here to learn and to teach, not to be sold to. Our goal for the website was to get visitors to understand right away that this wasn’t a normal tech conference. Our hallmark “Rockin’ Rooster” came out of a ~3 day back-and-forth with the team, where other ideas like “Rockin’ Grandma” were rejected in its favor. We felt the rooster represented something new, loud, and disruptive, in a good way. I used a free online SVG converter to turn the original crude cartoon into a scalable logo.We carried the same idea into the speaker pages. Every headshot got a uniform background and photo effect inspired by vintage concert posters. I worked out the look in ChatGPT, then built a small app in Kilo Code that applied it programmatically through the OpenAI image API, so every new speaker matched the rest without manual editing. It wasn’t long before people recognized the rooster before they even knew what the event was about, which is proof the branding landed.Trust the community to spread the word. This was our biggest growth lever. On a random weekday in September, I had the idea to ask my Dot (an AI agent I’ll explain below) to reach out to 3,000 tech groups, hackathons, and events around the world: anyone who might have a shred of interest in All Day AI. I proposed a free deal. Tell your community about our event, and I’ll put your logo, link, and CTA on our website. Hundreds responded. Based on rough estimates of community sizes, I would safely attribute 20-30% of our registrations to that one message. It worked because the offer cost nobody anything, and because a free, pitch-free event is something community organizers are happy to share.With those bets in place, the job became execution, and the tools we chose were all about saving the team’s time for the work only people could do.We wanted to spend as little time and money as possible on event infrastructure, so we looked for a platform that could natively handle 5 stages, registration forms, communications, and recording. We landed on Zuddl, which was modular enough to meet our requirements without us stitching together separate tools.Version 1 was built in Kilo Code for VS Code using GPT 5.6 and cost about $5. It was stored in GitHub, deployed to Vercel, and used Cloudflare for domain management. Because the speaker lineup and partner list changed constantly, the site had to change constantly too. The team and I made PRs as the event evolved, and I approved and merged them.Here’s where we had to get crafty. We wanted to attract top speakers across the AI industry, and quality speakers want a clear point of contact with a name and a quick response time. A shared, generic email address wasn’t going to cut it, so we used mine.That solved the trust problem and created a volume problem: one person fielding 140 speakers’ worth of email. To manage it, I used a series of AI agents with a human-in-the-loop editorial process. My Dot was the operating system for speaker communication. I gave it provisional access to Google Drive assets like the schedule and moderation Sheets and image collections, plus browser access to certain Zuddl lists and event settings. Then I had it send blasts and personalized speaker links, update Zuddl profiles, and manage moderation schedules. I stayed in the loop for every outgoing message, which let me track 140 speakers without holding the status of 140 email threads in my head. AI gets better with context, so the more I used the Dot, the more it understood the ADAI mission and the better it got at helping me. I let my Dot use the Kilo CLI on my computer to make site changes, which kept it more focused than asking it to generate GitHub PRs itself. When speaker information changed or I approved a new cohort, I asked the Dot to have Kilo update the site, so the website stayed in sync with the speaker list without a separate round of manual edits. Even with the Dot, my inbox became an absolute mess once we had about 20 of our 140 speakers. I gave Instinct, the agent that lives in iMessage, read-only access to my inbox and asked it to ping me whenever an urgent work item came in outside of All Day AI, so nothing from my day job got lost in the conference noise.Plans are one thing. Here’s what the two months looked like in practice, including the moments where it nearly fell apart.August 5–11: Concept and plumbing. A small group of the original core organizers outlined the event. A crude website appeared with placeholder registration, speaker, and volunteer forms while the team worked through platform, legal, and data requirements. We set the go-live date for October 22, 2026.August 16–25: A slow start. Responsibilities were assigned, and I took on speaker operations. Speaker intake, terms, platform setup, and partner materials were still being assembled. On August 25, we had 100 registrations and 12 speaker submissions, not even 1% of the final counts. With less than two months to go, we had a lot of ground to make up.August 28–September 11: Building in public. A readability-focused redesign prompted debate about losing the style of the first website. The first 22 speakers went up August 31, and a mobile registration issue was fixed September 3. Speakers didn’t just show up on their own; programming took active outreach and curation, with roughly 20 submissions awaiting review by September 11.September 14–30: The community takes over distribution. This is when the partner outreach started paying off. Community partnerships expanded through groups including AWT and NumFOCUS, and by September 28, registrations reached 2,725.October 12: The rehearsal humbles us. Registrations hit 5,864, but the dry run exposed how much we were still learning about Zuddl. Momentum and production readiness turned out to be separate problems, and we’d been solving the first one much faster than the second.October 13–16: A close call. A website-hosting payment warning forced a card replacement, and the site almost went down at the 11th hour. Speaker communications needed follow-up. By October 16, we had almost 8,900 registrations and 140 sessions locked, but we were still behind plan on registrations.October 18–19: Crossing the line. The count reached 9,961 late on October 18, just shy of our 10,000 goal. Speaker-access issues kept surfacing, so after working with platform support, we organized a last-minute series of dry runs.October 20–21: The run sheets land late. A preliminary moderator schedule circulated October 20, still dependent on available staffing. Full moderation schedules were finalized and posted at 9:40 p.m. the night before. By the end, the work was no longer about promotion at all; it was detailed human coordination.October 22: Event goes live. We finished with 12,313 registrants, 140 speakers, and an average watch time of more than 6 hours.Looking back at that timeline, most of the stress came in the last ten days, and most of it traces back to things we deferred while we chased registrations.Earlier, more frequent speaker ops. Because we were crunched for time, we prioritized carefully: once a speaker was on board, we considered them done and moved on to other operational work. We should have made time for multiple dry runs, kept up ongoing comms with speakers, and gotten earlier commitments to scheduled sessions. No-shows were low, but they weren’t zero, and we can plan for that next year.Platform training for moderators and volunteers. We were lucky to have most of the moderation team in person in Austin, so we could squeeze in a day of last-minute Zuddl training. It takes a lot of behind-the-scenes work to get a speaker prepped and on stage, and it would have been less stressful to train moderators and ushers further in advance, ideally before the October 12 rehearsal rather than after it.A dedicated speaker inbox. Reminder to myself for next year: don’t use my work email for speaker comms. The agents kept it manageable, but a separate, named inbox would have given speakers the same personal point of contact without burying my day job.All Day AI went from 100 registrations to more than 12,000 in about two months, built by volunteers, a $5 website, and a handful of agents. If you want to see what came out of it, you can watch all the recordings here. And if you want to be part of the next one, sign up for next year here.
